purpose: First-submission prose, with experimental identity and findings preserved

paragraphs.source_text: Abstract: Revon is a Python prototype for durable, linear-history key/value versioning. We study the choice between log aggregation and hash-pruned comparison over the same SQLite-backed fixed-depth Merkle trie. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of this choice and its workflow costs, rather than a new index or general-purpose database. Our author-run Linux evaluation of the JSON-repaired implementation comprises 516 executions and a separate 72-execution geometry/telemetry supplement. Eight of nine paired hybrid/Merkle timing intervals favour hybrid, while the dense case includes parity. A frozen threshold nevertheless selects a slower path in a separate control. The Windows evaluation comprises 93 cases, each run in a fresh worker process, with disjoint calibration and validation histories, controlled sensitivity experiments, Wine Quality and CO2 public sources, and repeated runs at 100,000 and 1,000,000 records. Its largest threshold candidate wins calibration and uses log throughout the tested intervals; this does not establish a benefit from switching or an optimal crossover. Published CO2 revisions provide observed record changes, while wine corrections remain generated. We report algorithm behaviour, CLI execution phases and whole-worker resources separately. All measured outputs and historical states are checked against semantic oracles. The results describe bounded versioning workflows on the recorded machines; they establish neither storage-engine superiority nor independent-party reproduction.
paragraphs.text: Abstract: Revon is a Python prototype for durable, linear-history key/value versioning. It supports log aggregation and hash-pruned comparison over the same SQLite-backed Merkle hash trie. We evaluate these two diff paths, an operation-count selection rule and the costs of complete versioning workflows. The Linux experiments comprise 516 executions and a separate 72-execution geometry and telemetry supplement. Eight of nine paired hybrid/Merkle timing intervals favour hybrid; the dense case includes parity. A separate threshold control selects Merkle when log is faster. The Windows evaluation covers 93 cases in fresh worker processes, with disjoint calibration and validation histories, controlled sensitivity experiments, Wine Quality and CO2 public sources, and repeated runs at 100,000 and 1,000,000 records. Its calibration winner uses log throughout the tested intervals, leaving the benefit of adaptive switching unresolved. CO2 supplies observed publication changes, whereas wine corrections are generated. We check diff outputs and historical states against semantic oracles and report algorithm, CLI-phase and whole-worker measurements with their respective boundaries. The findings describe trade-offs on the tested machines and histories. They do not establish an optimal crossover, storage-engine superiority or reproduction by an independent team.

paragraphs.source_text: A store that versions structured data needs to recover exact earlier states and compare them efficiently, even when updates affect only a few records. Simply archiving files does not provide all of these capabilities. Git links immutable, content-named objects through parent commits, offering a useful starting point [1]. Those objects represent files and directories. Record stores face a related problem: keys may remain in use while update density changes, and a comparison may cover just a few edits or many commits.
paragraphs.text: A versioned store for structured data must recover past states and compare them when only part of the data has changed. Saving complete files meets some of this need, but leaves record-level history and comparison to the application. Git provides a familiar model: immutable objects are identified by their content and connected through parent commits [1]. Those objects describe files and directories. A record store must also handle histories in which the same keys persist while update density and the number of intervening commits vary.

paragraphs.source_text: We investigate how two correct diff paths behave when they share the same fixed-depth Merkle hash trie, addressed operation history and durable representation. Path copying, cryptographic content addresses and SQLite transactions are established mechanisms. Our contribution is their explicit integration into an auditable comparison of selection policies, with matched semantic outputs and documented measurement boundaries. The scope is limited to the measured versioning operations and workloads, without implying lower costs for structured-data management generally.
paragraphs.text: We study two ways to compute a diff over a shared durable history. One aggregates operations from a log; the other prunes a Merkle hash trie using equal subtree hashes. Both use the same representation and return the same semantic output. Revon brings together established path-copying, content-addressing and SQLite transaction mechanisms so that we can compare these paths and a rule for selecting between them. The evaluation concerns the measured versioning operations and workloads, rather than the cost of structured-data management as a whole.

paragraphs.source_text: Dolt combines SQL with a commit graph and Prolly Trees [2], [3]. ForkBase contributes POS-Tree/SIRI storage and fork semantics [15], while Noms describes history-independent chunked collections [14]. Revon offers a narrower linear-history key/value prototype. We do not claim feature parity, a new family of persistent indexes, or a generally faster storage engine. The current comparison uses Revon's in-process API and Dolt's CLI; a separate phase breakdown makes the remaining interface costs explicit.
paragraphs.text: Dolt combines SQL, a commit graph and Prolly Trees [2], [3]. ForkBase provides POS-Tree/SIRI storage with fork semantics [15], and Noms describes history-independent chunked collections [14]. Revon focuses on a smaller interface: key/value operations over a linear history. Its purpose here is to support a controlled diff-path comparison, without claiming feature parity or a new family of persistent indexes. Cross-system measurements use Revon's in-process API and Dolt's CLI. We report the CLI phases separately to show the costs included in that comparison.

paragraphs.source_text: Implementation contribution: Revon integrates established content addressing, path copying and atomic SQLite persistence while exposing both diff paths under one encoded-value contract. This integration is an engineering contribution, not a claim to invent these mechanisms.
paragraphs.text: Implementation contribution: Revon combines content addressing, path copying and atomic SQLite persistence in a prototype that exposes both diff paths under one encoded-value contract. The engineering contribution is this integration and the ability to compare its paths under matched conditions.

paragraphs.source_text: Policy contribution: we specify and test an interpretable operation-count rule against its forced-path controls. The calibration choice is frozen before held-out evaluation; adverse choices and the possibility that always-log suffices are retained.
paragraphs.text: Policy contribution: we define an operation-count rule and compare its choices with both forced paths. Calibration is completed and the selected threshold recorded before held-out evaluation. The analysis includes adverse choices and considers whether always using log is sufficient for the tested histories.

paragraphs.source_text: Boundary of the contribution: the experiments concern single-writer linear histories and bounded workloads. They do not establish an optimal selector, a general geometry optimum, query-engine superiority or reproduction by an independent team.

paragraphs.source_text: A root digest in a Merkle tree authenticates the larger collection beneath it [4]. Content addressing appears in Git's software histories and in IPFS's networked content [1], [6]. Persistent data structures retain earlier states through path copying [5]. For dictionaries stored on disk, later designs include ordered stratified B-trees [16] and fully persistent B-trees [19]. Revon instead routes hashed keys through a fixed-depth trie. This allows hashes to prune a comparison, but sacrifices ordered range access. Scientific array systems take a different approach: SciDB and TimeArr use layouts and deltas suited to versioned arrays [17], [18]. Version access is also supported within a main-memory database by TardisDB, and replicated versioned structures for wide-area systems are studied by Saquib et al. [20], [21]. These designs help situate Revon's choices. They do not compare its log and Merkle paths on a common history.
paragraphs.text: A Merkle root authenticates the collection represented beneath it [4]. Git uses content addressing for software histories, while IPFS applies it to networked content [1], [6]. Path copying allows persistent structures to retain earlier states without copying everything [5]. Disk-oriented dictionaries include ordered stratified B-trees [16] and fully persistent B-trees [19]. Revon routes hashed keys through a fixed-depth trie: equal hashes can stop a diff traversal, but routing does not provide ordered range access. SciDB and TimeArr address versioned arrays through layouts and deltas suited to that setting [17], [18]. TardisDB supports version access in a main-memory database, and Saquib et al. study replicated versioned structures for wide-area systems [20], [21]. These studies explain several relevant design choices; they do not measure Revon's log and Merkle paths over a common history.

paragraphs.source_text: Merkle Search Trees use search-tree order and Merkle authentication to reconcile states [7]. Hashes also prune comparisons in Revon, but its routing is fixed-depth and its linear history is centralized, unlike a replicated CRDT. In LBFS, content-defined chunking identifies redundant content [8]. Dolt and Noms use related methods to choose boundaries. Such boundaries can improve deduplication when data shifts; ordered indexes, in turn, permit range operations. We evaluate neither of these capabilities in the Revon benchmark.
paragraphs.text: Merkle Search Trees combine search-tree ordering with Merkle authentication to reconcile states [7]. Revon also uses hashes to prune comparisons, but has fixed-depth routing and a centralized linear history rather than a replicated CRDT. LBFS uses content-defined chunking to find redundant content [8]; Dolt and Noms use related methods to determine chunk boundaries. Such boundaries can preserve deduplication as data shifts, while ordered indexes support range operations. Neither capability is evaluated by the Revon benchmark.

paragraphs.source_text: Dataset versioning must account for collaboration alongside the cost of storing and retrieving states. DataHub examines collaborative histories at scale [9]. Within a relational engine, Decibel supports branching and compares version-first, tuple-first and hybrid layouts [10]. OrpheusDB uses partitioning to improve version retrieval when versioning is added to an existing DBMS [11]. The storage/reconstruction trade-off is formalized by Bhattacherjee et al. [12]. Delta Lake builds ACID tables using transaction logs and checkpoints [13], while more recent work selects materialized versions and deltas on a version graph subject to storage and retrieval constraints [26]. Consistent identification and description of releases is the concern of the FAIR-compliant proposal [27]. It complements work on storage but does not specify a diff algorithm. Revon's key/value prototype covers a narrower problem and does not address these broader requirements of dataset management.
paragraphs.text: Dataset versioning involves collaboration as well as the cost of storing and recovering states. DataHub studies collaborative histories at scale [9]. Decibel supports relational branching and compares version-first, tuple-first and hybrid layouts [10]. OrpheusDB partitions data to improve version retrieval when versioning is added to an existing DBMS [11]. Bhattacherjee et al. formalize the storage/reconstruction trade-off [12]. Delta Lake uses transaction logs and checkpoints for ACID tables [13], and version-graph methods select materialized states and deltas under storage and retrieval constraints [26]. The FAIR-compliant proposal concerns consistent release identification and description [27], complementing storage work without specifying a diff algorithm. Revon's key/value interface addresses only part of this broader dataset-management problem.

paragraphs.source_text: Noms stores structured values in a Merkle DAG, with support for diff and synchronization [14]. In ForkBase, content addressing is combined with fork and deduplication semantics [15]. Dolt offers ordered indexing resembling a B-tree, structural sharing and native diff through content-addressed Prolly Trees [2], [3]. Git4Data supports snapshot, branch, diff and merge through SQL over a relational engine [29]. The manuscript available for that system is an arXiv preprint, so its reported results are not treated here as peer-reviewed or independently reproduced evidence. Revon's design is more limited. It uses fixed-depth hash routing in a single-writer key/value store with linear history, without SQL database capabilities or a branching system.
paragraphs.text: Noms represents structured values in a Merkle DAG and supports diff and synchronization [14]. ForkBase combines content addressing with fork and deduplication semantics [15]. Dolt provides structural sharing, native diff and ordered indexing through content-addressed Prolly Trees [2], [3]. Git4Data exposes snapshot, branch, diff and merge operations through SQL over a relational engine [29]. We use its available arXiv preprint to describe the abstraction, without treating the reported results as peer-reviewed or independently reproduced evidence. Revon has a narrower implementation: fixed-depth hash routing in a single-writer key/value store with linear history, without SQL or a branching interface.

paragraphs.source_text: Retaining history, creating versions and later reconstructing or comparing them each impose costs. Snapshots make retrieval straightforward by copying even the unchanged records. Logs postpone work until replay or checkpointing. Path copying retains the unchanged structure and creates only the paths that changed [5], [12]. Physical layout influences version creation and retrieval in Decibel and OrpheusDB [10], [11], while graph-based analyses express the storage/retrieval trade-off directly [26]. Reproducibility studies address the preservation of builds and artifacts for inspection [24]. Preserving them does not demonstrate that a storage algorithm runs faster, so we report import, commit, checkout, diff and storage separately.
paragraphs.text: Version creation, storage, reconstruction and comparison place work at different points in a history. Complete snapshots make retrieval simple but copy unchanged records. Logs defer work to replay or checkpointing. Path copying shares unchanged structure and creates the paths affected by an update [5], [12]. Decibel and OrpheusDB show how layout affects version creation and retrieval [10], [11]; version-graph analyses make the storage/retrieval trade-off explicit [26]. Reproducibility studies examine how builds and artifacts can be preserved for inspection [24]. We therefore record import, commit, checkout, diff and storage separately, and treat artifact preservation as a condition for inspection rather than evidence of faster execution.

paragraphs.source_text: The meaning of a change depends on the research question. Differential dataflow updates query results incrementally as timestamped inputs change [23]. Data provenance explains why and where output facts originated [22]; DSLog records fine-grained array lineage and supports queries over it [28]. Explain-Da-V explains semantic dataset changes through data transformations [25]. Baseline's operation-based differencing accommodates refactorings and schema changes [30]. Revon's output identifies keys that were added, removed or modified between two states. It does not explain causes, transformation lineage, query effects or schema intent. Although these studies help position the work, their outputs and workloads do not permit direct timing comparisons with Revon's key/value diffs.
paragraphs.text: A change can mean more than a difference between stored values. Differential dataflow updates query results as timestamped inputs change [23]. Provenance explains where output facts came from and why they occur [22]. DSLog records fine-grained array lineage and supports queries over it [28]. Explain-Da-V relates semantic dataset changes to transformations [25], while Baseline's operation-based differencing handles refactorings and schema changes [30]. Revon reports keys added, removed or modified between two states. It does not infer causes, lineage, query effects or schema intent. The related studies provide useful context, but their outputs and workloads do not support direct timing comparisons with these key/value diffs.

paragraphs.source_text: We compare two correct diff paths over the same durable history, choosing a path from properties of the requested interval. Every Revon-H commit retains a Merkle root and an addressed changeset, so selection leaves version semantics unchanged. Our hypothesis is that log aggregation works well for short, sparse intervals, whereas hash pruning may be useful after longer sequences of operations. Whether the paths cross in performance requires measurement; the switching rule alone cannot establish it. Git4Data illustrates continuing work on database-native version control [29]. Our contribution is confined to adaptive differencing over a fixed-depth hash trie, with Snapshot and Log-only serving as representation baselines. Revon is not a general-purpose data-versioning platform. The retained Linux public-record extension uses generated updates to one TLC release. The Windows evaluation uses generated wine corrections and an observed CO2 publication sequence. These bounded sources do not establish performance across diverse domains, independent hardware, concurrent workloads or production systems.
paragraphs.text: Each Revon-H commit stores a Merkle root and a content-addressed changeset. Either diff path can therefore recover the same endpoint changes, leaving the selection rule free to choose how that work is done. We hypothesize that log aggregation suits short, sparse intervals and that hash pruning may help after longer operation sequences. Whether their costs cross is an empirical question. Git4Data illustrates the broader interest in database-native version control [29]. Here, Snapshot and Log-only provide representation baselines for a fixed-depth-trie comparison. The public workloads use generated corrections to TLC and wine records, and observed changes in a CO2 publication sequence. These sources do not establish performance across independent hardware, concurrent workloads or production systems.

paragraphs.source_text: Trie nodes and changesets are serialized as canonical JSON, with each object's SHA-256 digest serving as its name. The commit digest includes the root, parent, changeset, message and timestamp. Readable labels such as v1 and v2 are aliases and have no effect on object identity. The current commit is identified by a durable HEAD reference.
paragraphs.text: Revon serializes trie nodes and changesets as canonical JSON and names each object by its SHA-256 digest. A commit's digest covers its root, parent, changeset, message and timestamp. Human-readable labels such as v1 and v2 are aliases, so they do not affect object identity. A durable HEAD reference identifies the current commit.

paragraphs.source_text: The main experiment uses b=8 and d=4. At each level, routing takes three bits from SHA-256(key); twelve bits select among 4,096 possible leaf buckets. Because a bucket retains the full keys, a shared routing prefix does not make two keys indistinguishable. With uniform hashes, expected bucket occupancy is N/b^d. We evaluate other b,d pairs separately and make no assumption that the default is optimal.
paragraphs.text: The main configuration uses b=8 and d=4. Routing consumes three bits of SHA-256(key) at each level, selecting among 4,096 possible leaf buckets with twelve bits. Leaves retain full keys, so keys with a shared routing prefix remain distinguishable. Expected occupancy is N/b^d under uniform hashing. We evaluate other b,d combinations separately rather than assuming that this default minimizes cost.

paragraphs.source_text: Revon first canonicalizes a mutation batch and routes its keys, grouping updates that share a trie prefix. It rewrites each affected leaf once and rebuilds the ancestors on those paths. Unchanged child hashes are carried into the new internal nodes, allowing the unchanged structure to be shared. One SQLite transaction writes the resulting objects and changeset, commit metadata, version alias and measurements, and updates HEAD. When the repository is reopened, Revon verifies stored payload hashes and references.
paragraphs.text: For a mutation batch, Revon canonicalizes the values and groups keys that share a routing prefix. It rewrites each affected leaf once, then rebuilds the ancestors along the affected paths. Internal nodes retain unchanged child hashes, allowing the corresponding structure to be shared. A single SQLite transaction writes the objects, changeset, commit metadata, version alias and measurements, and updates HEAD. Reopening a repository verifies stored payload hashes and references.

paragraphs.source_text: The log path walks the ancestry of the requested interval and combines operations for each key. The Merkle path compares the roots recursively: equal hashes end that part of the search, while differing paths lead to examination of their entries. Before choosing a path, Revon-H validates both version identifiers, checks ancestry in each direction and counts the changeset operations. An available ancestor path with a count no greater than T is eligible for log aggregation. Otherwise, Revon-H uses Merkle comparison. For a reverse request on the log path, it exchanges old and new values. A version compared with itself gives an empty diff. Forced log rejects unrelated versions, and an unknown version raises an error. Revon-M always requests the Merkle path, although its public API for a version pair still checks ancestry. Both paths return the same sorted semantic diff; commit and checkout are separate operations.
paragraphs.text: Log differencing walks the requested ancestor interval and combines operations by key. Merkle differencing compares roots recursively, stopping at equal hashes and examining entries below unequal paths. Revon-H first validates the version identifiers, checks ancestry in both directions and counts changeset operations. An eligible ancestor interval uses log when the count is no greater than T; otherwise it uses Merkle. Reverse log requests exchange old and new values, and identity requests return an empty diff. Forced log rejects unrelated versions, while unknown identifiers raise an error. Revon-M always requests Merkle, although its public version-pair API also checks ancestry. Both paths return the same sorted semantic diff. Commit and checkout are timed as separate operations.

paragraphs.source_text: We retain T=4,096 in the main Linux workflow matrix, as specified in the original workflow protocol. A separate Linux control tests the earlier frozen candidate, T=16,384. The threshold counts operations, whereas b^d specifies bucket capacity. We tune neither parameter from the Linux results.
paragraphs.text: The Linux workflow matrix uses T=4,096, as fixed by its protocol. A separate Linux control tests T=16,384, chosen by an auxiliary calibration experiment. The threshold counts operations; b^d determines bucket capacity. Neither parameter is fitted to the Linux results.

paragraphs.source_text: Revon accepts JSON nulls, booleans, finite numbers, strings, lists and objects whose keys are strings. It validates and detaches input containers before retaining them, and returns detached containers through read and diagnostic views. Immutable scalars may be shared. Before any write, it rejects Python-only values that are unsupported, non-string keys in nested objects, non-finite numbers and cyclic containers. Value equality follows the existing v1 JSON encoding, which uses sorted object keys, compact separators and UTF-8, with NaN excluded. The encodings of true, 1, 1.0 and signed floating zero therefore stay distinct. These rules define the Python encoding contract; they do not assert conformance to a cross-language canonical-JSON standard.
paragraphs.text: Revon accepts JSON nulls, booleans, finite numbers, strings, lists and objects with string keys. It validates and detaches input containers before storing them and returns detached containers from read and diagnostic views. Immutable scalars can be shared. Unsupported Python values, nested non-string keys, non-finite numbers and cyclic containers are rejected before a write. Equality follows the v1 JSON encoding: sorted object keys, compact separators, UTF-8 and no NaN. Thus true, 1, 1.0 and signed floating zero retain distinct encodings. This is the prototype's Python encoding contract, not a claim of conformance to a cross-language canonical-JSON standard.

paragraphs.source_text: Algorithm 1 (batch update). Validate the inputs and take ownership of their values. Before interning, reject overlapping puts/deletes and deletions of missing keys. Read the old values and keep only changes to encoded identity. Group these effective mutations by routing prefix, then rewrite each touched leaf, sort its entries and hash the complete payload. Rebuild the affected ancestors while reusing unchanged child hashes, and record the addressed changeset and commit. The ownership invariant prevents callers from changing retained values through earlier inputs or supported reads.
paragraphs.text: Algorithm 1 (batch update). Validate the batch and take ownership of its values. Before interning any object, reject keys present in both puts and deletes and requests to delete missing keys. Read the old values and retain mutations that change encoded identity. Group them by routing prefix, rewrite each touched leaf, sort its entries and hash its complete payload. Rebuild affected ancestors using unchanged child hashes where possible, then record the content-addressed changeset and commit. Detaching values ensures that callers cannot alter stored history through input containers or supported reads.

paragraphs.source_text: Algorithm 2 (log composition). Traverse the ancestor interval chronologically. For each key, keep the existence/value at its first old endpoint and at its last new endpoint. Drop that key only if both endpoints agree in existence and encoded value. Thus, inserting and then deleting a key cancels, as does updating and then restoring its value; a null value is still distinct from an absent key. Sort the remaining keys. A reverse request exchanges the endpoints and swaps the added/deleted labels.
paragraphs.text: Algorithm 2 (log composition). Traverse the ancestor interval in chronological order. For each key, retain its existence and value at the first old endpoint and the last new endpoint. Remove it from the result only when both endpoints agree in existence and encoded value. An insertion followed by deletion cancels, as does an update followed by restoration. A null remains different from an absent key. Sort the remaining keys; for a reverse request, exchange endpoints and swap the added/deleted labels.

paragraphs.source_text: Algorithm 3 (selection). Validate the versions and check ancestry in either direction. Add the changeset operation counts across the interval. Choose log for an eligible interval whose count is at most T, and Merkle otherwise. Merkle comparison skips addressed subtrees with equal hashes and compares values in unequal leaves. Both paths use the same encoded-identity rule and return detached outputs.
paragraphs.text: Algorithm 3 (selection). Validate the version pair and check ancestry in either direction. Sum changeset operation counts over the interval. Select log for an eligible interval with a count at most T, and Merkle otherwise. Merkle traversal skips equal-hash subtrees and compares values in unequal leaves. Both paths apply the same encoded-identity rule and detach returned values.

paragraphs.source_text: Cost model. Let N denote the record count, d the depth, b the branching factor, m the keys in a batch, h the interval length, p the accumulated operations, u the distinct interval keys and s the serialized output bytes. Expected leaf occupancy under uniform routing is N/(b^d), with N as the worst case. Processing a batch involves validating and copying inputs, performing m routed lookups of old values and scanning the occupied leaves. Touched leaves must be sorted and serialized, and affected internal child maps must be copied. The work therefore cannot be bounded by a dataset-independent O(d).
paragraphs.text: Cost model. Let N be the record count, d the depth, b the branching factor, m the keys in a batch, h the interval length, p the accumulated operations, u the distinct interval keys and s the serialized output bytes. Under uniform routing, expected leaf occupancy is N/(b^d); in the worst case it is N. A batch must validate and copy inputs, perform m routed old-value lookups and scan occupied leaves. Touched leaves are sorted and serialized, and affected internal child maps are copied. These costs prevent a dataset-independent O(d) bound for batch processing.

paragraphs.source_text: Log composition includes ancestry traversal and O(p + u log u) work, together with encoded-value comparisons and output copying/serialization. For Merkle comparison, the work depends on the node pairs visited, sorting child slots and the leaf entries examined, as well as comparing values and sorting the output. Both public version-pair modes traverse ancestry. A reverse request may initially walk to genesis in the direction that fails. Producing the output costs at least an amount proportional to s. Larger JSON values introduce comparison and copying costs beyond those characterized by scalar-only benchmarks.
paragraphs.text: Log composition traverses ancestry and performs O(p + u log u) work, in addition to encoded-value comparisons and output copying/serialization. Merkle cost depends on the node pairs visited, child-slot sorting and leaf entries examined, followed by value comparison and output sorting. Both public version-pair modes traverse ancestry. For a reverse request, the unsuccessful direction may first walk to genesis. Output construction requires work at least proportional to s. Large JSON values add comparison and copying costs that scalar-only benchmarks do not characterize.

paragraphs.source_text: Historical nodes, changesets and commits are loaded eagerly from SQLite into memory. Although the repository stores its objects durably, they are resident while Revon runs, and the retained history must fit in memory. The amount of retained payload determines the work of opening and verifying a repository. No disk-page cache or eviction policy is provided. The atomicity of SQLite persistence does not demonstrate the production concurrency or operational guarantees that we have not tested.
paragraphs.text: Revon loads retained nodes, changesets and commits eagerly from SQLite. Objects are durable on disk but resident while the prototype runs, so the retained history must fit in memory. Opening and verifying a repository also depends on its retained payload. There is no disk-page cache or eviction policy. SQLite transaction atomicity provides a persistence mechanism; production concurrency and operational guarantees require tests beyond this evaluation.

Appendices A and B explain access and give the detailed procedures.

paragraphs.source_text: The variants retain history in different ways. Snapshot stores a complete state at every version; Log-only stores the starting state and subsequent operations. Revon-M requests Merkle diff, whereas Revon-H chooses its diff path. Dolt uses a primary-key SQL table and returns native JSON diff. For Dolt, SQL INSERT and CSV table import are timed separately, giving six workflow variants across five systems. Their later operations follow the same semantic contract, although their interfaces and storage features differ. The figures use the workload identifiers assigned in Table 4.
paragraphs.text: The five systems provide six workflows. Snapshot stores a full state at each version; Log-only stores an initial state and subsequent operations. Revon-M requests Merkle diff, and Revon-H selects a path. Dolt stores records in a primary-key SQL table and returns its native JSON diff. We time SQL INSERT and CSV table import as separate Dolt workflows. Subsequent operations follow the same semantic output contract despite differences in interfaces and storage features. Table 4 defines the workload IDs used in the figures.

paragraphs.source_text: Eight synthetic scenarios, each with six variants, two warm-ups and seven measured trials, account for 432 executions. The public-record cases contribute 27 executions across Revon-M, Revon-H and Dolt SQL, and the two threshold controls contribute another 54. Three million-row diagnostics bring the campaign to 516 executions: 114 warm-ups, 399 measured trials and three diagnostics. All 516 finished with verified outputs. Failed timing executions are not silently replaced or omitted.

paragraphs.source_text: The public-data extension uses NYC TLC's January 2024 yellow-taxi release [31]. A checksum fixes the Parquet input, which has 2,964,624 rows. With seed 20261001, we use a dispersed affine permutation to obtain nested subsets of 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 rows. We retain eleven fields: vendor, pickup/drop-off times, passenger count, distance, pickup/drop-off locations, payment type, fare, tip and total. Each key is formed from the release, the file-checksum prefix and the physical row ordinal. It identifies a row within this fixed file, not the same trip in different releases. Values, including nulls, are serialized as compact UTF-8 JSON with sorted keys. In the million-row subset, 47,277 passenger counts are missing, and serialization succeeds for every row. Identical field values do not cause rows to be combined. The affine permutation used for sampling is not uniformly random.
paragraphs.text: The TLC workload uses the January 2024 yellow-taxi release [31], whose checksum fixes a Parquet input of 2,964,624 rows. A dispersed affine permutation with seed 20261001 produces nested subsets of 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 rows. We retain eleven fields: vendor, pickup/drop-off times, passenger count, distance, pickup/drop-off locations, payment type, fare, tip and total. Keys combine the release, file-checksum prefix and physical row ordinal. They identify records within that file, without asserting trip identity across releases. Values, including nulls, use compact UTF-8 JSON with sorted keys. The million-row subset contains 47,277 missing passenger counts; every row serializes successfully. Identical field values do not merge rows. This affine sampling procedure is not uniformly random.

paragraphs.source_text: We generate the public edit histories with ten commits. On the 100,000-row subset in the Linux campaign, a commit makes 100 corrections; in the million-row diagnostic, it makes 1,000. A correction adds 0.01 to both fare and total, leaving the other retained fields untouched. All systems receive identical records and mutations. These edits are constructed for the experiment and are not observed longitudinal changes. The public-data builder ignores the inherited payload_bytes=8 field in the configuration. All eleven fields remain in a public value, and payload size is accounted for through the measured serialized bytes. The harness stores a canonical record as a JSON-encoded string in the common value column. We therefore do not measure native mutation of nested objects or queries on individual fields.
paragraphs.text: We construct ten-commit TLC histories. Each commit changes 100 records in the Linux 100,000-row workload and 1,000 records in the million-row diagnostic. A correction adds 0.01 to fare and total while leaving other retained fields unchanged. All systems receive identical inputs and mutations. These are generated edits, not observed trip revisions. The public-data builder ignores the configuration's inherited payload_bytes=8 field and retains all eleven source fields; measured serialized bytes determine payload size. Each canonical record is stored as a JSON-encoded string in the common value column. The experiment therefore measures neither native nested-object mutation nor queries on individual fields.

Audits reconstruct the plan and semantic hashes; they verify internal consistency, not a fresh timing experiment.

These differently conditioned values are not pooled or interpreted as pure tree overhead.

Sensitivity cases vary rows, history interval, payload, geometry and routing in a prespecified staged design. Holding accumulated operations fixed makes interval length trade off against changes per commit, so the design is not fully factorial. The appendices and protocols specify all seeds and matched controls.

paragraphs.source_text: Key takeaways
paragraphs.text: Answers to the research questions

paragraphs.source_text: RQ1: the workflow measurements expose latency, persistence and worker-resource trade-offs, with API/CLI costs still preventing an engine-only ranking. RQ2: some fixed histories benefit from log relative to forced Merkle, but the Windows calibration winner uses log everywhere tested; optimal switching remains unestablished. RQ3: controlled sensitivity histories make payload, routing and geometry effects visible within the tested design, without identifying a universally best layout. Observed CO2 transitions broaden revision realism, while generated wine and synthetic histories retain their own scope limits.
paragraphs.text: For RQ1, the complete workflows show trade-offs in latency, persistent storage and worker resources, while API/CLI boundaries prevent an engine-only ranking. For RQ2, log helps on several fixed histories, but the Windows calibration winner selects it everywhere tested; an advantage from adaptive switching remains unestablished. For RQ3, controlled histories reveal payload, routing and geometry effects within the staged design without identifying a universal layout. Observed CO2 transitions provide a different kind of history from generated wine corrections and synthetic updates, and each source retains its own scope limits.

paragraphs.source_text: RQ1 concerns the complete versioning contract. The Linux and local experiments both retain import, commit, diff, checkout and persistent footprint, but their rows are analysed separately. Snapshot and Log-only expose representation costs; the M/H/log controls hold the Revon representation fixed. Dolt provides a richer SQL/versioning interface. Its command-phase decomposition improves transparency without making its native tree cost comparable to an isolated Python tree call.
paragraphs.text: The workflow results address RQ1 at the interface used by an application. Both Linux and Windows experiments measure import, commit, diff, checkout and persistent footprint, but their rows are analysed separately. Snapshot and Log-only expose representation costs; forced M, H and log comparisons hold Revon's representation fixed. Dolt supplies a richer SQL/versioning interface. Reporting its command phases makes the workflow easier to inspect without equating its native tree work to an isolated Python call.

paragraphs.source_text: RQ2 concerns transfer to unseen histories, not merely repeated timing of one history. The Windows split controls primary N, H, payload and geometry and freezes selection before validation. Its largest candidate behaves as always-log within the measured interval range. The adverse Linux selection and dense-case parity remain useful counterexamples. A more complex selector would require new calibration and untouched testing; these results do not justify adding complexity or changing the production threshold.
paragraphs.text: RQ2 requires testing transfer beyond the histories used to select a parameter. The Windows split holds primary N, H, payload and geometry fixed and records selection before validation. Its largest candidate behaves as always-log over the measured range. The adverse Linux threshold choice and dense-case parity show why the rule cannot be assumed to choose the fastest path. A more complex selector would need separate calibration and untouched testing. These findings do not justify changing the default threshold.

paragraphs.source_text: RQ3 concerns controlled changes to the fixed trie and its workload. Equal-capacity geometries can differ in traversal depth and ancestor reconstruction while having equal expected occupancy under uniform routing. Payload encoding, touched leaves and output materialisation also contribute. The Windows sensitivity set uses independent seeds and matched controls alongside the Linux study of one fixed history, but does not estimate every factor interaction or a population optimum.
paragraphs.text: For RQ3, geometries with equal capacity can have different traversal depths and ancestor-reconstruction costs despite equal expected occupancy under uniform routing. Payload encoding, touched leaves and output construction also affect latency. Windows cases use separate generated seeds and matched controls, while the Linux geometry experiment holds one history fixed. Neither design estimates every interaction or a population-wide optimum.

paragraphs.source_text: The JSON repair is included in every current Linux experiment. Previously, mutable aliases could remain connected to stored values. Python equality could also treat true as equal to 1, or 1 as equal to 1.0. We repaired those semantics by detaching inputs and outputs and comparing v1 encoded identities, keeping the object encoding and on-disk schema intact. Archived earlier timings describe the implementation before this repair. The Linux trials exercise the repaired source on the supplied histories, and unit tests cover null/absence, nested ownership, unsupported values and rollback.
paragraphs.text: Value semantics matter to a valid diff comparison. Revon detaches inputs and outputs so that mutable aliases cannot alter stored history. Its v1 encoded identities distinguish true from 1 and 1 from 1.0, while preserving the object encoding and on-disk schema. Linux trials exercise these semantics on the supplied histories. Unit tests additionally cover null versus absence, nested ownership, unsupported values and rollback.

paragraphs.source_text: External validity: Linux results come from one author-run cloud VM, and Windows results from one author-run host. Both campaigns were conducted by the authors; the Windows campaign does not reproduce the Linux environment. Hardware, OS, runtime, virtualization and storage vary together between campaigns. Background services and filesystem caching remain active; the local manifest records limited available RAM and process conditions. No entirely idle, cold-cache or OS-causal claim follows.
paragraphs.text: External validity: the authors ran Linux experiments on one cloud VM and Windows experiments on one local host. These are not independent-party replications or controlled OS comparisons. Hardware, runtime, virtualization and storage change together. Background services and filesystem caching remain active; the Windows manifest also records limited available RAM and process conditions. The study does not represent an entirely idle or cold-cache host.

paragraphs.source_text: Workload validity: the original TLC histories remain generated from one monthly release, with n=1 Linux scale diagnostics. The Windows evaluation includes three held-out generated seeds per primary profile, generated wine corrections and one observed CO2 publication sequence. Three CO2 repositories repeat that sequence rather than independently sampling its history. A header-only upstream revision is excluded before timing, and unnamed columns are retained without scientific interpretation. Repeated synthetic scale histories broaden observations but share their initial distribution. More domains, observed histories and hardware are still needed for broad generalisation.
paragraphs.text: Workload validity: TLC histories contain generated updates to one monthly release, and Linux scale diagnostics have n=1 per system. Windows validation uses three held-out generated seeds per primary profile, generated wine corrections and one observed CO2 publication sequence. Three CO2 repositories repeat that sequence rather than sampling independent histories. A header-only revision is excluded before timing; unnamed columns are retained without scientific interpretation. Synthetic scale histories share their initial distribution. Broader generalization requires more domains, observed histories and hardware.

paragraphs.source_text: Implementation scope: Revon uses a trie of fixed geometry and loads retained nodes, changesets and commits eagerly, without evicting them from memory. It supports a single writer and linear history. We have not evaluated named branches, merge commits, conflict handling, schema evolution, remotes, ordered scans, crash fault injection or concurrent workloads. The use of atomic SQLite transactions does not, by itself, demonstrate all the durability and operational guarantees needed in production.
paragraphs.text: Implementation scope: the fixed-geometry trie loads retained nodes, changesets and commits eagerly, without eviction. Revon supports one writer and linear history. Named branches, merge commits, conflict handling, schema evolution, remotes, ordered scans, crash fault injection and concurrent workloads are outside this evaluation. Atomic SQLite transactions alone do not establish all durability or operational guarantees needed for production use.

paragraphs.source_text: Measurement and inference: process startup, native work and JSON emission remain combined in Dolt's command interval. Whole-worker RSS includes oracle/history state and is not product-only memory. Ten-millisecond sampling can miss short-lived processes, and Windows I/O counters do not identify physical-disk or database logical reads. The off/on sampler diagnostic also confounds execution order and cache state. The historical bootstrap intervals concern fixed-history timings; Windows three-history ranges are descriptive and have no multiple-comparison correction. Source and semantic-hash checks establish internal consistency, not independent performance reproduction.
paragraphs.text: Measurement and inference: Dolt command time combines process startup, native work and JSON emission. Worker RSS includes oracle and history state, and ten-millisecond sampling can miss brief processes or peaks. Windows I/O counters measure neither physical-disk traffic nor database logical reads. Sampler off/on comparisons also confound order with cache conditions. Linux bootstrap intervals describe repeated fixed-history timings; Windows three-history ranges are descriptive, without multiple-comparison correction. Source and semantic-hash checks establish internal consistency, not independent timing reproduction.

paragraphs.source_text: Selection and design: calibration is limited to four thresholds, two generated seeds and the declared primary profiles. T=65,536 is the largest candidate and does not switch within the tested operation range. That outcome leaves a broadly useful adaptive selector unestablished. The staged sensitivity design is not a full factorial; H and density trade off at fixed operation count, and hash-route tests require their own low-density control. A new selector or crossover claim requires a separately frozen experiment.
paragraphs.text: Selection and design: the primary Windows calibration covers four thresholds, two generated seeds and the specified profiles. The largest candidate, T=65,536, does not switch within the tested range, so broad usefulness of adaptive selection remains unestablished. The staged sensitivity design is not fully factorial: H trades off against density at fixed operation count, and hash-route cases need their matched low-density control. Establishing a different selector or crossover requires a separately fixed experiment.

paragraphs.source_text: Possible storage changes include binary nodes, value chunks, packed objects, compression and reachability-based garbage collection. Range operations could be supported through an ordered Merkle index or content-defined chunking. Each proposal needs its own semantic and performance evaluation; its effects cannot be inferred from the fixed-trie results presented here.
paragraphs.text: Possible storage extensions include binary nodes, value chunks, packed objects, compression and reachability-based garbage collection. An ordered Merkle index or content-defined chunking could support a different range-operation design. Each change would require its own semantic and performance evaluation; the fixed-trie results do not predict its effects.

paragraphs.source_text: Revon integrates established fixed-trie content addressing, changesets and atomic SQLite persistence to expose two semantically consistent ways to compute a version diff. The retained Linux evidence comprises 516 executions and a 72-execution supplement, including dense-case uncertainty and an adverse threshold choice. The Windows evaluation comprises 93 worker cases and 3,402 checked queries, with held-out generated histories, Wine Quality and CO2 public sources, interface-phase measurements and repeated scale observations. Calibration selects T=65,536, which behaves as always-log in this matrix and does not establish optimal switching. The combined evaluation covers controlled workload variations and public data while retaining API/CLI, sampling, dataset and hardware limits. The contribution is an auditable prototype and a bounded empirical trade-off study; a new general-purpose database, universal speed advantage and independent-party reproduction are not established.
paragraphs.text: Revon provides two semantically consistent diff paths over content-addressed fixed-trie history stored atomically in SQLite. The contribution is an inspectable prototype and an empirical comparison of its workflow and selection costs. Linux evidence covers 516 executions and a separate 72-execution supplement, including dense-case uncertainty and an adverse threshold choice. Windows experiments comprise 93 worker cases and 3,402 checked queries across held-out histories, Wine Quality and CO2 sources, interface phases and repeated scale runs. Calibration selects T=65,536, which always uses log in the tested primary matrix. This outcome leaves an optimal crossover unresolved. The results support conditional trade-offs for the recorded workloads, with API/CLI, sampling, dataset and hardware limits. They establish neither a universal speed advantage nor independent-party reproduction.

Measurement starts only after restoring that empty fixture directory and passing the complete suite. The setup failure remains in the execution records.

paragraphs.source_text: For every primary execution, we start a fresh worker and create a repository. The protocol records model order, which is shuffled deterministically and rotated within repetition blocks. Import timing ends when the first durable version has been created. The reported incremental-commit time is the median of the individual commit timers for that history. A diff runs from the first version to the last and returns sorted changed keys, together with old/new value hashes, as canonical JSON. Checkout writes the complete sorted key/value state in canonical UTF-8 JSON. A Dolt timer includes launching the CLI, parsing JSON and normalizing the output. Revon is called through its in-process API. This difference in timing boundaries prevents a speed claim about the engines alone.
paragraphs.text: Each primary execution starts in a fresh worker and constructs a repository. Model order is deterministically shuffled and rotated within repetition blocks. Import ends when the first durable version exists. Incremental-commit latency is the median of the individual commit timers for that history. Diff compares the first and last versions and emits sorted changed keys with old/new-value hashes as canonical JSON. Checkout writes the full sorted key/value state as canonical UTF-8 JSON. Dolt timing includes CLI launch, JSON parsing and output normalization; Revon uses an in-process API. The different boundaries prevent interpreting workflow ratios as engine-only speed comparisons.

paragraphs.source_text: We perform correctness checks outside the operation timers. In every primary execution, we verify the hashes of the initial and final states, check all H+1 historical states, and compare the observed canonical semantic diff with a workload oracle constructed independently. The verification JSON retains observed and expected hashes, rather than just an expected count of changed keys. The post-run audit regenerates workloads and checks the exact matrix, the selected paths and the identity of the source, data and protocol. It also recomputes all summaries. We audit the downloaded evidence locally as well. These procedures check internal integrity; they do not constitute an independent reproduction of the timings.
paragraphs.text: Correctness checks run outside operation timers. Each primary execution verifies initial and final state hashes, every H+1 historical state and the observed canonical diff against a separately constructed workload oracle. Verification records contain both observed and expected hashes. The audit regenerates workloads, checks matrix membership, selected paths and source/data/protocol identities, and recomputes summaries. Downloaded records are also audited locally. These checks establish internal integrity rather than an independent repetition of the timing experiment.

paragraphs.source_text: We exclude warm-ups and report the median and interquartile range (IQR) of the seven measured repository trials. For a latency ratio, we first pair the trials, then report the median ratio and a paired percentile bootstrap interval from 20,000 resamples. Values above one favour the denominator. These exploratory 95% intervals describe repeated timings of a fixed workload on one VM. They are not population confidence intervals, and we apply no multiple-comparison correction. Taking the median of paired ratios need not give the same value as dividing the two latency medians. We retain every completed trial, including timing outliers.
paragraphs.text: After excluding warm-ups, we report medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs) over seven measured repository trials. For latency ratios, matched trials are paired before calculating the median ratio and a paired percentile-bootstrap interval from 20,000 resamples. Values above one favour the denominator. The exploratory 95% intervals concern repeated timings of a fixed workload on one VM, without a population or multiple-comparison interpretation. The median of paired ratios can differ from the ratio of the two latency medians. Every completed trial, including timing outliers, remains in the record.

paragraphs.source_text: The parent process samples the worker and its descendants every 10 ms, recording RSS, CPU and I/O counters. Peak measurements include workload generation, the oracle state and verification along with the storage work. They cannot be assigned to the storage engine alone. A short peak or a short-lived subprocess's counters can fall between samples. The original sampler treats an all-zero read counter as missing, so we draw no read-I/O conclusion from the primary campaign. In a separate supplement, we distinguish a recorded zero from an unavailable counter and retain those data apart from the primary results. A cached workload can examine logical data while recording zero physical read bytes.
paragraphs.text: A parent process samples worker and descendant RSS, CPU and I/O every 10 ms. Peaks include workload generation, oracle state, verification and storage work; they cannot be assigned to the storage engine alone. Brief peaks or short-lived subprocesses can fall between samples. The primary Linux sampler records an all-zero read counter as missing, so those records support no read-I/O conclusion. The supplementary campaign distinguishes measured zero from unavailable counters and is analysed separately. Cached data can be examined logically while the process records zero physical read bytes.

paragraphs.source_text: We measure repository footprint as directory size before closing or compacting it. This includes indexes, metadata and the costs of the representation. Logical payload normalization and selected compaction probes from the first trial are also retained. These measurements describe the workflow rather than isolating tree overhead. CPU, RSS and I/O span the full worker lifecycle, giving them a different scope from the individual operation timers.
paragraphs.text: Linux repository footprint is directory size before closing or compaction, including indexes, metadata and representation costs. Records also provide logical-payload normalization and selected first-trial compaction probes. These describe the complete workflow rather than tree overhead alone. CPU, RSS and I/O cover the worker lifecycle, a wider boundary than the individual operation timers.

paragraphs.source_text: The earlier Windows study evaluated thresholds of 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192 and 16,384 operations on predefined calibration and validation profiles that did not overlap. Minimizing normalized calibration latency selected T=16,384 before validation. Its held-out normalized score was 1.032, against 1.297 for T=4,096; always-log scored 1.000 in both splits. These cached-query measurements belong to their archived source and environment, and do not measure the repaired Linux implementation. Selection of the largest candidate in the search does not identify an optimum. The earlier long-history and three-seed pilots are retained as exploratory supplementary evidence.
paragraphs.text: The auxiliary Windows threshold experiment uses non-overlapping predefined calibration and validation profiles and candidates of 1,024, 2,048, 4,096, 8,192 and 16,384 operations. Minimizing normalized calibration latency selects T=16,384 before validation. Its held-out normalized score is 1.032, compared with 1.297 for T=4,096; always-log scores 1.000 in both splits. These cached-query results belong to that experiment's recorded source and environment and are separate from Linux timings. A largest-candidate winner does not identify an optimum. Long-history and three-seed pilot records provide exploratory context.

paragraphs.source_text: In the Linux threshold control, T=16,384 remains frozen. We use 10,000 rows and 512 changes per commit, with H=16 and H=64 giving 8,192 and 32,768 accumulated operations. Forced log, forced Merkle and hybrid are run in separate workers, each with two warm-ups and seven measured trials. We do not change the threshold in response to Linux results. These two cases check how the existing choice carries over to Linux, without constituting a new calibration/validation cycle.
paragraphs.text: The Linux threshold control fixes T=16,384 over 10,000 rows with 512 changes per commit. H=16 and H=64 produce 8,192 and 32,768 accumulated operations. Forced log, forced Merkle and hybrid use separate workers, with two warm-ups and seven measured trials each. The threshold is not selected from Linux outcomes. These cases test transfer of the auxiliary calibration choice, rather than performing another calibration/validation cycle.

paragraphs.source_text: The geometry supplement uses a single spread workload: 10,000 rows, ten commits, 100 changes per commit, 32-byte synthetic values and seed 20260824. Diff is fixed to forced Merkle for b4-d6, b8-d3, b8-d4, b8-d5 and b16-d3. Each configuration runs in a fresh worker for two warm-ups and seven measured trials. We rotate the order to limit confounding between configuration and time. Every execution checks the eleven historical states and endpoint diff outside the timers. Geometry timings follow the same adapter output contract, but the resource peaks measured by its inherited in-process monitor are kept separate from the external RSS measurements.

It then confirms that the original collection hashes remain intact. The archive provides these checks and acquisition recipes; they validate evidence consistency rather than elapsed times or a new research team's reproduction.
